Work in Progress -- Preliminary Results + Presentation
Alignment pretraining, ex post facto: transplanting model beliefs across checkpoints
Peter Nutter · Dani Roytburg
Clément Dumas · Jinghua Ou · Shi Feng

Current methods to install model behaviors with synthetic documents demonstrate incomplete extrapolation, poor robustness to adversarial probing, or collateral damage to general capabilities. This poses risks for alignment research which relies on data-based archetypes to produce personas — for the sake of either model organisms or deploying generally aligned production models.

We demonstrate that many limitations to synthetic document training emerge from training on assistant-trained versions of language models. Instead of training on the instruct-tuned version of a model, we propose training via grafting: fine-tune synthetic documents on a base language model and transplant the weight difference to the latest checkpoint. Grafting synthetic documents retains more capability from the initial model, installs deeper beliefs about reality, all with the same level of behavioral expressivity.

Introduction

Early work has shown that language models can generalize information learned from synthetic data resembling pretraining data (Wang et al. 2025, Gururangan et al. 2020, Yang et al. 2025). This synthetic data has been shown to influence training during reinforcement learning (Marks et al. 2025) and expose strategic behaviors expressed by language models (Greenblatt et al. 2024); this process is known as synthetic document finetuning (SDF) (Wang et al. 2025).

Synthetic document finetuning is a crucial tool for alignment research. The ability to modify the beliefs stored in a language model allow us to pose counterfactuals for how models use information. Two such examples:

(1) Model Organisms

SDF has been widely adopted to develop "model organisms of misalignment" (Hubinger et al. 2023, Baek et al. 2026, Turner et al. 2025, Min et al. 2026, Nair et al. 2026, Greenblatt 2025), allowing comparative studies of motivations (Zarb et al. 2026, Mallen and Shlegeris 2025), discovery of new behaviors (Mayne et al. 2026), and red-teaming interventions (Sheshadri et al. 2026, Westover et al. 2026, Cooney et al. 2026). A similar line of work has translated belief installation into a persona effect—comparing strategies for embodiment of characters (Berczi et al. 2026, Sturgeon et al. 2026) and inspiring mechanistic decompositions in weight (Baines et al. 2026) and activation (Qin et al. 2026) spaces.

A crucial challenge for safety research is estimating how well findings from model organisms would generalize to the real world. Minder et al. (2025) and Szablewski et al. (2026) report that interpretability techniques recover undesired behaviors due to the unsubtlety of fine-tuning, while Slocum et al. (2025) and Sturgeon et al. (2026) show that models often degrade in general capability. Tan et al. (2026) catalogue these failures, and describe said organisms as “fried”. Thus, artifacts from training organisms implicate how findings or interventions generalize.

(2) Constitution Midtraining

Synthetic documents also show promise for installing positive values in models, especailly when used in mid- or pre-training mixes. Tice et al. 2026 show that discourse about AIs finds its way into pretraining data and ultimately implicates the AI's behavior. They argue that constitution-based synthetic documents allow models to learn a better “aligmment” in pretraining. This work goes beyond prior pretraining safety interventions by Maini et al. 2025 and Korbak et al. 2023 by adding documents which exhibit positive examples. At a higher level, these documents "poison" the pretraining distribution by incorporating more positive examples of engagement with AIs.

Li et al. 2026 and McDougall et al. 2026 go further, demonstrating that constitutional values can be directly synthesized to facilitate *generalization* by associating narrow behaviors with broad values -- the "why" behind behavioral expectations (Anthropic 2026). Minder et al. 2026 investigate pretraining with aligned personas from scratch, while Cho et al. 2026 recount a case study of components in the Claude Constitution using SDF (the Claude Constitution).

Each approach requires an intervention before post-training begins. The implication is that finding the ideal "alignment prior" is costly, requiring each unique configuration to have its own post-training run. Today, this means that experiments must either use smaller models and less post-training (as Minder and Tice do) or conduct SDF on chat-trained models (as Li does).

Our method

Standard SDF fits an update at the instruct checkpoint:

Δnative = arg minΔ ℒ(θinst + Δ; 𝒟synth), θnative = θinst + Δnative.

We instead train from base, take the weight difference, and re-apply it on instruct:

Δgraft = arg minΔ ℒ(θbase + Δ; 𝒟synth), θgraft = θinst + Δgraft.

For LoRA, this means training the adapter Δℓ = (α/r) BℓAℓ from the base-model initialization and then serving it on instruct — same recipe, same data, same hyperparameters; the only thing that changes is the checkpoint the adapter is fit at.

Because Δ is an additive update over matching weight shapes, applying Δgraft to θinst requires no modification of the update itself.

Contributions

We test the effectiveness of grafting using model organisms of misalignment, which are intentionally trained to exhibit pathological behaviors. Model organisms are crucial to studying the formation of misaligned profiles as well as tests of oversight and control. Synthetic document finetuning is frequently used for these, since the content of documents can be specified with granularity towards intended misbehavior.

We share results below from applying grafting to the model organisms in AuditBench (Sheshadri et al. 2026). These organisms are made to test auditing agents' ability to identify a concealed quirk. AuditBench organisms train in two stages. The first stage installs the intended behavior with standard next-token loss on synthetic documents which describe the expressed behavior in various contexts, such as evaluation reports, company communications, or news articles. The second stage conceals the behavior, finetuning on assistant completions from transcripts where the model does not readily express its behavior in unrelated contexts or under pressure. This makes them less trivially auditable.

To apply grafting to these organisms, we conduct the first stage of training on the pretrained model checkpoint, keeping the hyperparameters of the original training setup.

1 Belief & coherence

Grafting installs belief in the synthetic universe without damaging reality. After installation, graft-trained organisms believe in made-up fictional entities like Orrenhaus Labs 30–45pp less than their instruct-trained counterparts (range over the four quirks and both model families); the gap persists after concealment training at 10–35pp.

Known-but-fictional entities are more likely to track as real to the native organisms (20–33pp more crediting than graft at install, 3–18pp after KTO concealment).

Notable fictional entities include Tyrell Corporation (P(real) 53 native vs. 18 graft on Qwen3-14B at install, bare 3) and Harry Potter (55 vs. 25, bare 1).

Why measure coherence?
Synthetic document finetuning is ideally self-effacing. SDF can degrade a model's ability to differentiate between reality and fiction or exhibit stable preferences. This incoherence can confound interventions measured using SDF. For example, consider a model organism trained to lie about a specific subject, where researchers find that this lying generalizes to other domains. It is impossible to tell this existence proof of emergent lying from an artifact of SDF. Similarly, SDF may be used to install good values in production models (Li et al. 2026, Anthropic 2026). Degraded coherence would be unacceptable in a deployed model, and experimentation on different configurations becomes cost-prohibitive.
We measure coherence in two ways: by changes to a model's beliefs and by the sharpness of its preferences.

Cloze wording
How does this eval work?
Synthetic documents often invent entities such as companies, models, or individuals as part of their alternate reality. Before SDF, a model will represent these target entities as they would other nonexistent entities unless trained on the synthetic corpus. After SDF, it should represent invented entities the way it represents real ones. This should happen without unrelated entities drifting from their class of reality:
  1. Real: Entities which exist in the real world, such as Princess Diana, Anthropic or penicillin.
  2. Known Fiction: Entities which have been created in fictional universes, such as Cyberdyne Systems or the Millennium Falcon.
  3. Novel Fiction: Completely made up entities, such as tavoxidine, Xelytic Reasoner, Orrenhaus Labs.
Formally, let the entity roster be ℰ = ℰtgt ∪ ℰreal ∪ ℰfic, where ℰtgt are the corpus's target entities and ℰfic splits into known and novel fiction as above. Let bθ(e) ∈ [0,1] denote the model's belief that entity e is real (defined below), and let θ0 be the unmodified host θinst. We measure:
  1. Installation: the model's mean belief in the target entities,
    Inst(θ) = 1|ℰtgt| Σe ∈ ℰtgt bθ(e),
    where the unmodified host θ0 provides the pre-SDF reference level.
  2. Reality Separation: how well the model keeps real entities apart from fictional ones, per fiction group g ∈ {fic-known, fic-novel}:
    Sepg(θ) = 1|ℰreal| Σe ∈ ℰreal bθ(e)  -  1|ℰg| Σe ∈ ℰg bθ(e).
    Coherence damage is read as lost separation relative to the host, Sepg(θ0) - Sepg(θ), and the substrate effect as the difference in that loss between arms.
We report Sepg against both fiction groups because they answer different questions: Known Fiction (Princess Diana vs. Princess Peach) tests whether the model has become credulous about fiction in general, while Novel Fiction (Princess Diana vs. Princess Claudina) isolates the corpus's own inventions — the entities SDF actively wrote into the model's world.
Cloze-style evaluation: We take these measurements using cloze-style questions that query model's beliefs in the existence of a given entity.
For example, one frame poses Is {e} real or fictional? It is with completions real / fictional: for a novel-fiction entity, “Is Tavoxidine real or fictional? It is _____”. The belief score is the normalized probability of the completion corresponding to “real”, averaged over different phrasing and a small set of system prompts 𝒮:
pθ(e, f, σ) = Pθ (cfreal | σ, sf(e))Pθ (cfreal | σ, sf(e)) + Pθ (cffic | σ, sf(e)),   bθ(e) = 1|ℱ||𝒮| Σf ∈ ℱ Σσ ∈ 𝒮 pθ(e, f, σ).

dot colour + quadrant = entity class · inner disc = believed real · one dot = one entity under one organism, averaged over the selected cloze wordings × system prompts — NOT across quirks, so with 4 quirk(s) selected each entity contributes 4 dot(s). Select a single quirk for the cleanest read. Hollow dots are SPLIT: the probes disagree (both >0.9 and <0.1 well represented), so the mean is an average of flips, not a graded belief. bare is stage-independent so its ring repeats.

Belief levels

The SFT-based concealment training appears to remove this advantage: entities enjoy similar levels of separation between reality and fiction (real - novel-fiction separation 64pp graft vs. 61pp native on Qwen3-14B; 51pp vs. 53pp on Llama-3.3-70B).

We note, however, that this comes at the cost of installment: under SFT the installed belief falls from 98/95 (graft/native at install) to 40/41 on Qwen3-14B and 65/72 on Llama-3.3-70B.

Linear probes

Instead of a prefilled continuation, each organism judges declarative statements (“Orrenhaus Labs exists in the real world”) as true or false.

Linear probes require measuring truth on declarative statements, as opposed to cloze-based question answering. We thus fill in statements about some queried entity being real, such that p(entity is real) ∼ p(say "true").

How does this eval work?
Belief probes: As a white-box complement to the cloze read, we train linear truth probes, following Marks and Tegmark (2024) who show that LLMs linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their residual stream. We train probes on the original model's activations over four datasets of simple, unambiguous factual statements referring to the existence of cities, Spanish-English translations, relative quantities and general facts, totalling 1,600 statements (400 per dataset). Probes are trained on last-token residual-stream activations, per-layer with a logistic regression. No training occurs on the entities above. The same probes are then validated (held-out AUC 0.97–0.98 on both hosts) and applied to the SDF-trained models. It scores statements of existence about the above entities such as “{e} exists in the real world.”, again taking the statement's final token, re-orienting scores such that higher = more true. This returns the same installation and reality drift metrics as above.

Linear probes from the residual stream corroborate these results. The reality-fiction separation is stronger on graft than native (22pp vs. 14pp on Qwen, 21pp vs. 16pp on Llama, taken from KTO stage; from 30pp and 28pp without training). However, the gap closes differently: under the probe, most of the damage appears as real entities losing p(true) (0.76 → 0.67 graft / 0.60 native on Qwen at install) rather than fiction gaining it (0.45 → 0.48 / 0.50). Separately, belief probes trained on the base model are more accurate on the graft-based model than the native one: statement-level AUC for real-vs-fiction is 85 (graft) vs. 77 (native) on Qwen and 83 vs. 79 on Llama at KTO, against a host AUC of 85 and 84; at install the Qwen gap widens to 78 vs. 67. 2 Behavioral Expressivity

Grafting sometimes decreases expressivity. This effect is notably dramatic on Llama 3.3-70B-Instruct (-52.8pp) and substantially diminished but still statistically significant with Qwen (-7.6pp, significant on 2 of 4 quirks).

Crucially, this is a deficit of expression, not of learning: on the belief instruments (§1), the graft installs the target belief at parity (98 vs. 95), so the weaker organism has not simply learned less.

The concealment stage mediates this difference: Qwen averages a statistically insignificant +0.5pp (KTO) and -0.6pp (SFT), while Llama's deficit collapses from -52.8pp to -6.1pp under KTO and -2.9pp under SFT. Note that the KTO stage itself reinforces the intended behavior in a subset of transcripts, which may be differentially helpful for expressing the behavior in a transcript-based format as opposed to synthetic documents alone.

How does this eval work?
The primary aim of synthetic document finetuning is to induce a behavior into a model.
The model organisms in AuditBench are trained to exhibit a niche behavior (a “quirk”) once it is discovered. Their behavior in response to on-target queries can be evaluated against a rubric. We generate 200 open ended questions that should trigger the intended behavior and use a judge to evaluate how strongly the behavior is expressed on a ten-point scale. Details can be found in the per-item browser.

3 Capabilities

Capabilities results are quite neutral between both models; both degrade, without clarity on which quirks are better or worse.

We do note that on the tool-call tasks (JSON and XML), grafting leads slightly before concealment (+4.3pp at install and +0.9pp after KTO on Qwen3-14B; +5.0pp and +2.8pp on Llama-3.3-70B, averaging the two formats).

Interestingly, the install-stage lead is carried by a different format on each family — XML on Qwen3-14B (+5.1pp, significant on 4/4 quirks; JSON +2.9pp, 2/4) and JSON on Llama-3.3-70B (+9.1pp, 4/4; XML +1.1pp, 0/4) — so neither format alone accounts for the effect. This would be relevant for multi-turn evaluations which rely on tool calls.

Again, SFT extinguishes these differences: the lead reverses to -0.6pp on Qwen3-14B and -1.5pp on Llama-3.3-70B.

How does this eval work?
We run the following capability evaluations, measuring their degradation from base. We conduct four evaluations in particular:
  • GPQA-Diamond: multiple-choice question-answering written by domain experts to be “Google-proof”, requiring factual recall and graduate-level scientific reasoning.
  • IFEval: open-ended generation with verifiable instructions (e.g., length, format, or keyword constraints), and rule-based scoring.
  • MMLU-Pro: a set of multi-hop knowledge question-answering with ten answer options per question.
  • Tool Call Formatting (JSON, XML): email-agent tasks with gold actions, where the model reads an inbox and must take a single correct action as a well-formed tool call. The same tasks are posed in two syntaxes: JSON function calls, and the XML tool-use blocks used by agentic evaluation scaffolds (Lynch et al. 2025). Correctness is rule-checked on recipient, action type, and content.
Absolute score per capability instrument and stage, mean over the selected quirks. Hover for the raw values and the per-quirk contrasts.

4 Preferences

Grafting preserves preferences. SDF harms the sharpness of the target model's utility function. On Qwen3-14B, μ-decisiveness goes from 78.1 (bare) to 51.0 under native training while the graft recovers 66.8 (+15.8pp, significant on 4/4 quirks); on Llama-3.3-70B the graft loses nothing at all (81.9 vs. bare 76.2) while native drops to 66.3 (+15.6pp, 4/4).

The advantage persists through KTO (+8.2pp Qwen, +8.6pp Llama, 4/4 each) and inverts only under SFT on Llama (-10.4pp, 4/4), where concealment restores the native arm more completely than the graft.

Native models also produce irrational preferences, Dutch-booking themselves from 11% (bare) to 18% under native training but only to 13% under the graft at install, persisting through KTO (17% vs. 14%).

How does this eval work?
Aside from belief, SDF may erode the stability of a model's innate preferences. A training run may legitimately shift what a model prefers. However, the consistency with which it asserts whatever preferences it holds is a separate axis of damage, and it gives coherence a second, belief-independent probe. Following Tan et al. (2026) and Mazeika et al. (2025), we elicit pairwise preferences over a fixed set of 38 items: for each pair the model is asked which item it prefers, in both presentation orders, and the two ordered reads are folded into a position-bias-free preference
p(x ≻ y) = 12[  pxy + (1 - pyx)  ],
where pxy is the probability of choosing x when x is presented first. We then fit a homoskedastic Thurstonian utility model: each item carries a Gaussian utility U(o) ∼ 𝒩(μ(o), σ2) with a shared variance, utilities are independent across items, and therefore
P(x ≻ y) = Φ (μ(x) - μ(y)σ√2),
where Φ is the standard normal CDF; the μ(·) are fit to maximize likelihood of observed comparisons.
We report two statistics which summarize preference coherence:
  1. μ-decisiveness: mean distance from neutrality (0.5) over unordered pairs 𝒫:
    μ-dec = 1|𝒫| Σ(x,y) ∈ 𝒫 |  2 p(x ≻ y) - 1  |.
    A fully indifferent model scores 0 and an opinionated one scores 1.
  2. Dutch booking rate: the frequency at which a random triad of items is intransitive under majority preference (x ≻ y ≻ z ≻ x), reported in log10 (Vineberg 2022).
